meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The secret of managing is to keep the guys who hate you away from the ones who are undecided'?
meta.ogDescription: Widely credited to Casey Stengel — but no dated source has ever been found, and the earliest printing we could reach is a 1976 book, about a year after he died.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1890–1975 · Baseball manager — Yankees, Mets · Hall of Fame, 1966
answer.sourceLine: Everyone credits Stengel, including the institutions that ought to know: the National Baseball Hall of Fame ↗ and SABR ↗ both print a version of it as his answer when asked how he managed. Neither gives a date, a game, a column or a page — and no primary source has been found carrying this sentence in Stengel’s own recorded words.

source.excerpt: The secret of managing is to keep the guys who hate you away from the ones who are undecided.
trail: The National Baseball Hall of Fame ↗ gives the line as Stengel’s reply when asked to divulge his managerial strategy, in the form “Keep the five guys who hate you away from the five who are undecided.” It attaches no date and no source. SABR’s BioProject essay ↗ carries the identical five-and-five wording, also uncited — the two most authoritative baseball bodies repeat the same sentence and neither says where it came from.

Wikiquote’s Casey Stengel page ↗ sources every entry to a dated newspaper or book, and does not carry this line at all. The nearest thing it does source is a different remark on the same theme, from the December 1964 Winter Meetings: Stengel broke a club into a first fifteen who need no managing, a next five to butter up, and a last five “plotting to get you fired.” That is recalled by Cleveland Press reporter Bob Sudyk in The Hartford Courant of 14 March 1993.

Searching the Internet Archive’s scanned-book index for the phrase returns only secondary repetitions — quotation anthologies, business and management titles, joke collections — never a contemporaneous report of Stengel saying it. The earliest printing we could reach is Bob Woolf’s Behind Closed Doors (Atheneum, 1976) ↗, about a year after Stengel died, in the form “the five players who hate you away from the five who are undecided.” The earliest printings we found that attach his name are two 1979 anthologies, Sports Quotes (Omnibus Press) ↗ and Caught by Keating (Deutsch) ↗ — both giving “hate your guts,” both uncited. That index holds books only, not newspapers, so this is a floor on the printed record rather than a firm first appearance.
source.excerptNote: No fuller context survives, because no source records the moment it was said. The form above is one of several in circulation; Baseball Almanac ↗ prints it with “the guys who are undecided,” while Goodreads ↗ has “the folks who hate you away from the ones who haven’t made up their minds yet.”

Nothing here should be read as a public-domain clearance: if the line really is Stengel’s, the first publication that captured it is unknown, and the anthologies that carry it today are themselves in copyright.

author.name: Casey Stengel
author.kicker: The man it is pinned on
author.heading: Casey Stengel
author.metaLine: 1890–1975 · Outfielder turned manager · Ten pennants in twelve Yankee seasons
author.bio: Charles Dillon “Casey” Stengel was born in Kansas City in 1890, reached the majors with Brooklyn in 1912, and finished playing with the Boston Braves in 1925 before starting over as a manager. His first two decades in the job went mostly badly — the Dodgers 1934–1936, the Braves 1938–1943 — and then the Yankees hired him in October 1948 and he won ten pennants in twelve seasons, including five consecutive World Series titles from 1949 through 1953. He closed out with the expansion Mets from 1962 to 1965 and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1966. Sportswriters called him the Ol’ Perfessor, and his looping, digressive way of talking is a large part of why so many crisply-worded aphorisms ended up with his name under them.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: Almost nobody credits this to anyone but Stengel — though at least one 1979 anthology prints a variant under Billy Martin’s name. What goes wrong is subtler: a line with no source has been repeated so confidently, for so long, that it now reads as documented when it never was.

items.why: Both the Hall of Fame ↗ and SABR ↗ print it as his, and neither supplies a date, an interviewer or a publication. Two authoritative repetitions of an uncited sentence do not add up to a source.

Across the Internet Archive’s book index the count shifts between five-and-five and five-and-four, “undecided” swaps with “haven’t made up their minds,” and “guys” becomes “folks,” “people” or “ones.” The exact form asked about here — the ones who are undecided — is genuinely rare, while the numberless “guys … guys” version is the commonest of all, which is why this page’s wording reads almost like a slip of it. (Exact-phrase item counts in that index, retrieved September 2026: numberless 136, five-and-five 86, five-and-four 19, this page’s form 3.)

Stengel really did have a documented theory of managing a twenty-five man roster, and it is not this sentence: it splits the club into fifteen, five and five, and it is sourced on Wikiquote ↗ to the 1964 Winter Meetings via a 1993 Hartford Courant recollection. The famous one-liner looks like a tightened, anonymous rewrite of that idea, but no source connects them.

Sports Quotes (Omnibus Press, 1979) ↗ prints “Keep the five players who hate you away from the four who are undecided” under “Billy Martin, baseball manager” — while crediting a near-identical line to Stengel elsewhere in the same volume; Sportswit (1984) repeats the Martin credit. Martin played for Stengel’s Yankees and later managed them himself, which is the likeliest route for the two names to blur. It is a thin claim against an overwhelming Stengel consensus, but it is a claim, and it is in print.

misattribution.truthLine: Honest verdict: probably Stengel, provably nobody’s documented words. Until someone turns up a dated column, broadcast or book page, the strongest true statement is that the Hall of Fame ↗ credits him and the record does not confirm him.

context.heading: Why a manager would say it
lead: Stengel spent twelve seasons deciding which of twenty-five men played, and the arithmetic of that job is brutal: nine start, the rest wait, and resentment collects at the far end of the bench. A manager who lasted as long as he did was managing the unhappy as much as the talented.

That is why the line rings true even without a source. It is not really about hatred — it is about containment: keep the aggrieved from recruiting the merely uncertain, and you keep a clubhouse. The trouble is that a sentence being plausible is exactly what lets it travel unchecked for forty years.
context.detailsSummary: Why a quote like this is so hard to pin down
detailsBody: Stengel is one of the most quotable figures in American sport, and “Stengelese” was famously loose — long, circling, self-interrupting. Reporters routinely tidied him up for print. A polished epigram in his mouth is therefore always suspect: the neater the sentence, the likelier a writer shaped it.

There is also a structural gap in the evidence. Full-text search covers scanned books well and newspapers poorly, so a line that first ran in a 1950s sports column could sit unindexed while its later anthology reprints surface instantly. The 1976 date below is the earliest printing we could reach, not a claim about where the line began.
context.pull: Probably Stengel. Provably nobody’s documented words.

sourcesVerified.claim: The National Baseball Hall of Fame prints "Keep the five guys who hate you away from the five who are undecided" as Stengel's reply when asked to divulge his managerial strategy, with no date or source attached.

SABR's BioProject biography carries the identical wording, uncited, and gives Stengel's dates (30 July 1890 – 29 September 1975) and his managerial record including Yankees 1949–1960 and Mets 1962–1965.

Wikiquote's Casey Stengel page sources every entry and does not contain this quote; the nearest sourced line is his December 1964 Winter Meetings remark breaking a club into fifteen, five and five, via Bob Sudyk in The Hartford Courant, 14 March 1993.

Baseball Almanac prints the popular short form — "The secret of managing is to keep the guys who hate you away from the guys who are undecided" — with no source, while citing books and dates for other quotes on the page.
Goodreads carries the variant "The secret of managing is to keep the folks who hate you away from the ones who haven't made up their minds yet," credited to Casey Stengel with no work cited.

Full-text search of the Internet Archive's scanned books for this phrase returns only secondary repetitions — quotation anthologies, business and management titles, joke collections — with no period reportage. Exact-phrase item counts retrieved 8 Sep 2026 via openlibrary.org/search/inside.json: "the guys who hate you away from the guys who are undecided" 136; "the five guys who hate you away from the five" 86; "the five guys who hate you away from the four" 19; "hate you away from the ones who are undecided" 3.

Bob Woolf's Behind Closed Doors (New York: Atheneum, 1976) contains "to keep the five players who hate you away from the five who are undecided" — the earliest printing of the line located in the Internet Archive scanned-book index, about a year after Stengel's death, and the only hit for that exact wording.

Sports Quotes, eds. Don Atyeo and Jonathon Green (London: Omnibus Press, 1979), prints "keep the five players who hate your guts away from the five who are undecided. Casey Stengel, baseball manager" and, separately in the same volume, "Keep the five players who hate you away from the four who are undecided. Billy Martin, baseball manager" — the earliest Stengel-credited printing located, and the earliest competing credit.

Caught by Keating: Sporting Quotations from the Seventies (London: Deutsch, 1979) prints "keep the five players who hate your guts away from the five who are undecided. Casey Stengel, US baseball manager", uncited.

The Executive's Quotation Book: A Corporate Companion, edited by James Charlton, was published by St. Martin's Press in 1983 and is scanned by the Internet Archive; its full text contains the five-and-five variant of the quote.

Casey Stengel was born 30 July 1890 and died 29 September 1975; he won ten pennants in twelve Yankee seasons including five straight World Series 1949–1953, managed the Mets 1962–1965, and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1966.
